claim: During continuous speech, lip movements provide visual temporal signals that facilitate speech processing.
source: During continuous speech, lip movements provide visual temporal signals that facilitate speech processing.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a premise for the study.

claim: There is significant entrainment between oscillatory brain activity and speaker's lip movements in visual cortex.
source: First, we investigated coherence between oscillatory brain activity and speaker's lip movements and demonstrated significant entrainment in visual cortex.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on MEG data analysis.

claim: Attending visual speech enhances the coherence between activity in visual cortex and the speaker's lips.
source: Comparing this synchronization between different attention conditions revealed that attending visual speech enhances the coherence between activity in visual cortex and the speaker's lips.
evidence: This finding is based on comparing partial coherence across different attention conditions in the MEG data.

claim: There is a significant partial coherence between left motor cortex and lip movements that directly predicts comprehension accuracy.
source: Further, we identified a significant partial coherence between left motor cortex and lip movements and this partial coherence directly predicted comprehension accuracy.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on partial coherence analysis and regression with behavioral data.

claim: Visually entrained and attention-modulated rhythmic brain activity is important for the enhancement of audiovisual speech processing.
source: Our results emphasize the importance of visually entrained and attention-modulated rhythmic brain activity for the enhancement of audiovisual speech processing.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Movements of the lips contain sufficient information to allow trained observers to comprehend speech through visual signals.
source: Movements of the lips contain sufficient information to allow trained observers to comprehend speech through visual signals.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Lip movements can be beneficial for speech comprehension when the acoustic signal is degraded.
source: Even for untrained observers and in the presence of auditory signals, lip movements can be beneficial for speech comprehension when the acoustic signal is degraded (Peelle and Sommers, 2015; Sumby and Pollack, 1954; van Wassenhove et al., 2005; Zion-Golumbic and Schroeder, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Dynamic lip movements support disambiguation of syllables and can provide temporal onset cues for upcoming words or syllables.
source: Dynamic lip movements support disambiguation of syllables and can provide temporal onset cues for upcoming words or syllables (Chandrasekaran et al., 2009; Grant and Seitz, 2000; Kim and Davis, 2003; Schroeder et al., 2008; Schwartz and Savariaux, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Synchronization of brain rhythms between interlocutors has been implicated in the encoding of acoustic speech.
source: A potential underlying mechanism for the visual enhancement of hearing could be the synchronization of brain rhythms between interlocutors, which has been implicated in the encoding of acoustic speech (Giraud and Poeppel, 2012; Hasson et al., 2012; Pickering and Garrod, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Continuous speech and the associated lip movements show temporal modulations at the syllabic rate (3–8 Hz).
source: Indeed, continuous speech and the associated lip movements show temporal modulations at the syllabic rate (3–8 Hz) (Chandrasekaran et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Previous studies have demonstrated the frequency-specific synchronization between brain activity and continuous auditory speech signals at frequencies below 10 Hz.
source: Consistent with this idea, previous studies have demonstrated the frequency-specific synchronization between brain activity and continuous auditory speech signals (Ahissar et al., 2001; Ding and Simon, 2012; Gross et al., 2013b; Luo and Poeppel, 2007; Peelle et al., 2013) at frequencies below 10 Hz.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Synchronization to auditory speech was found to be stronger for intelligible than non-intelligible speech.
source: This synchronization was found to be stronger for intelligible than non-intelligible speech and facilitated by top-down signals from left inferior frontal and motor areas (Ding and Simon, 2014; Kayser et al., 2015; Park et al., 2015) as well as during attention (Zion-Golumbic and Schroeder, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Auditory speech entrainment and speech intelligibility are enhanced when congruent visual speech is present.
source: This is plausible as the auditory speech entrainment and speech intelligibility are enhanced when congruent visual speech is present (Crosse et al., 2015; Zion Golumbic et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Participants showed high comprehension accuracy across all experimental conditions (All congruent: 85 ± 1.66%, All incongruent: 77.73 ± 2.15%, AV congruent: 83.40 ± 1.73%, AV incongruent: 75.68 ± 2.88%).
source: Overall, participants showed high comprehension accuracy across conditions (%; mean ± s.e.m.): All congruent: 85 ± 1.66, All incongruent: 77.73 ± 2.15, AV congruent: 83.40 ± 1.73, AV incongruent: 75.68 ± 2.88).
evidence: This is a direct report of behavioral data from the experiment, also shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Accuracy was significantly higher when the visual stimulus was congruent with attended auditory stimulus compared to when the visual stimulus was incongruent with attended auditory stimulus.
source: As expected, accuracy was significantly higher when the visual stimulus was congruent with attended auditory stimulus (i.e., All congruent and AV congruent conditions) compared to when the visual stimulus was incongruent with attended auditory stimulus (i.e., All incongruent and AV incongruent conditions) (Figure 1B; paired t-test, df: 43, p<0.05; All congruent vs. All incongruent: t = 3.09, p=0.003, All congruent vs. AV congruent: t = 0.76, p=0.45 (n.s.), All congruent vs. AV incongruent: t = 2.98, p=0.004, AV congruent vs. All incongruent: t = 2.15, p=0.03, AV congruent vs. AV incongruent: t = 2.24, p=0.03, All incongruent vs. AV incongruent: t = 0.65, p=0.52 (n.s.)).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Performance for AV congruent condition was not significantly different to performance in All congruent condition despite the interfering auditory input.
source: Interestingly, performance for AV congruent condition was not significantly different to performance in All congruent condition despite the interfering auditory input.
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of behavioral data.

claim: The lip signal is dominated by low-frequency components from 0 to 7 Hz peaking around 0 to 4 Hz.
source: The signal is dominated by low-frequency components from 0 to 7 Hz peaking around 0 to 4 Hz (Figure 2B; from all lip speech signals used in this study; mean ± s.e.m.).
evidence: This is based on spectral analysis of lip signals shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The coherence spectrum between lip signals and acoustic signals reveals a prominent peak in a frequency band corresponding to the syllable rate around 4–8 Hz.
source: The coherence spectrum reveals a prominent peak in a frequency band corresponding to the syllable rate around 4–8 Hz (red line; mean ± s.e.m.) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on coherence analysis between lip and sound signals shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There is temporal coupling of auditory and visual speech components.
source: These results demonstrate the temporal coupling of auditory and visual speech components.
evidence: This is inferred from the coherence analysis between lip and sound signals.

claim: Natural audiovisual speech (All congruent condition) shows significant entrainment effect in visual, auditory, and language areas bilaterally at 1 Hz.
source: We first compared natural audiovisual speech condition (All congruent) and surrogate data for the frequency that showed strongest power in the lip signal (1 Hz). This revealed a significant entrainment effect in visual, auditory, and language areas bilaterally (p<0.05, false discovery rate (FDR) corrected; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on coherence analysis comparing real data to surrogate data, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The entrainment areas include early visual (V1; Calcarine sulcus) and auditory (A1; Heschl's gyrus) areas as well as inferior frontal gyrus (IFG; BA 44).
source: The areas include early visual (V1; Calcarine sulcus) and auditory (A1; Heschl's gyrus) areas as well as inferior frontal gyrus (IFG; BA 44) (see Figure 2—figure supplement 2 for the other conditions at 1 Hz).
evidence: This is based on anatomical localization of the entrainment effects shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Sound speech envelope entrainment reveals an extensive auditory network including Heschl's gyrus and superior/middle temporal gyri bilaterally and left frontal areas.
source: In accordance with previous work (Gross et al., 2013b), we observed an extensive auditory network including Heschl's gyrus and superior/middle temporal gyri bilaterally and left frontal areas (p<0.05, FDR corrected; Figure 2E)(see Figure 2—figure supplement 3 for different frequencies [2–5 Hz]).
evidence: This is based on coherence analysis with sound speech envelope shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Statistical comparison of lip movement entrainment to sound speech entrainment revealed significantly stronger lip entrainment in bilateral visual areas and stronger sound speech coherence in right superior temporal gyrus.
source: Statistical comparison of lip movement entrainment (Figure 2D) to sound speech entrainment (Figure 2E) revealed significantly stronger lip entrainment in bilateral visual areas and stronger sound speech coherence in right superior temporal gyrus (p<0.05, FDR corrected; Figure 2F).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of two coherence maps shown in Figure 2F.

claim: There is significant entrainment of brain activity to the lip movements irrespective of entrainment to the acoustic speech signal.
source: This demonstrates significant entrainment of brain activity to the lip movements irrespective of entrainment to the acoustic speech signal.
evidence: This is inferred from the statistical comparison showing distinct patterns of entrainment.

claim: There is significant lip movement entrainment in visual areas in the absence of a congruent auditory stimulus.
source: In addition, we found significant lip movement entrainment in visual areas in the absence of a congruent auditory stimulus (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the All incongruent condition shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: This study demonstrates for the first time the entrainment of cortical brain oscillations to lip movements during continuous speech.
source: These results demonstrate for the first time the entrainment of cortical brain oscillations to lip movements during continuous speech.
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding of the study.

claim: AV congruent condition shows significantly stronger lip movement entrainment at 4 Hz in the left visual cortex compared to both All congruent condition and surrogate data.
source: This revealed significantly stronger lip movement entrainment at 4 Hz in the left visual cortex for AV congruent compared to both, All congruent condition and surrogate data.
evidence: This is based on partial coherence analysis in visual ROI shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Coupling of low-frequency brain activity to lip movements is enhanced by visual attention.
source: This result suggests that coupling of low-frequency brain activity to lip movements is enhanced by visual attention.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of attention conditions.

claim: Attended audiovisual speech leads to significant entrainment in left inferior precentral gyrus corresponding to the lip representation in motor cortex.
source: Attended audiovisual speech leads to significant entrainment in left inferior precentral gyrus corresponding to the lip representation in motor cortex (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D) (Giraud et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on coherence analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D with citation support.

claim: Partial coherence analysis reveals a more superior left lateralized motor area when the effect of speech envelope on lip entrainment is removed.
source: In addition, partial coherence analysis where the effect of speech envelope on lip entrainment is removed reveals a more superior left lateralized motor area (Figure 3B,C,D).
evidence: This is based on partial coherence analysis shown in Figure 3B,C,D.

claim: Partial coherence in left motor cortex is modulated by congruence and attention.
source: Partial coherence in this area is modulated by congruence (Figure 3C) and attention (Figure 3D) and predicts comprehension accuracy (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on partial coherence analysis across conditions and regression with behavior shown in Figures 3C, 3D, and 4A.

claim: Left motor areas are not only activated but also entrained by audiovisual speech.
source: Our results indicate that left motor areas are not only activated but also entrained by audiovisual speech.
evidence: This is inferred from the partial coherence findings in motor cortex.

claim: Entrainment establishes a precise temporal coupling between audiovisual sensory inputs and sensory and motor areas that could temporally coordinate neuronal computations associated with speech processing.
source: This establishes a precise temporal coupling between audiovisual sensory inputs and sensory and motor areas that could temporally coordinate neuronal computations associated with speech processing.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the entrainment findings.

claim: Motor areas could provide access to an internal forward model of speech that closely interacts with auditory sensory systems as part of a proposed dorsal auditory pathway.
source: As part of a proposed dorsal auditory pathway, motor areas could provide access to an internal forward model of speech that closely interacts with auditory sensory systems (Bornkessel-Schlesewsky et al., 2015; Rauschecker and Scott, 2009).
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation supported by citations.

claim: During speech production, an efference copy is sent to auditory areas to allow for efficient monitoring and control.
source: During speech production, an efference copy is sent to auditory areas to allow for efficient monitoring and control.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about speech production.

claim: During speech perception, sensory signals could be used to constrain the forward model in simulating the speaker's motor program and predicting upcoming sensory events.
source: During speech perception, sensory signals could be used to constrain the forward model in simulating the speaker's motor program and predicting upcoming sensory events (Arnal and Giraud, 2012; Bornkessel-Schlesewsky et al., 2015; Lakatos et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation supported by citations.

claim: A recent study has demonstrated direct top-down control of left auditory cortex from left motor cortex during continuous speech processing.
source: Indeed, a recent study has demonstrated direct top-down control of left auditory cortex from left motor cortex during continuous speech processing.
evidence: This claim is introduced with reference to previous research.

claim: The strength of low-frequency top-down signals in the left motor cortex correlates with the coupling of auditory cortex and sound speech envelope.
source: The strength of low-frequency top-down signals in the left motor cortex correlates with the coupling of auditory cortex and sound speech envelope (Park et al., 2015) (see also Kayser et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The motor cortex plays a predictive role in speech perception consistent with recent demonstrations of its contribution to the temporal precision of auditory speech perception.
source: This suggests that the motor cortex plays a predictive role in speech perception consistent with recent demonstrations of its contribution to the temporal precision of auditory speech perception (Morillon et al., 2014; 2015; Wilson et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Visual speech per se is not critical for speech comprehension, however, it facilitates auditory speech processing as it aids temporal prediction and can prime the auditory system for upcoming concordant auditory input.
source: Visual speech per se is not critical for speech comprehension, however, it facilitates auditory speech processing as it aids temporal prediction and can prime the auditory system for upcoming concordant auditory input (Peelle and Sommers, 2015; van Wassenhove et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Left motor cortex seems to be an important area for facilitating audiovisual speech processing through predictive control in auditory active sensing.
source: Overall, left motor cortex seems to be an important area for facilitating audiovisual speech processing through predictive control in auditory active sensing (Meister et al., 2007; Morillon et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings with citation support.

claim: Entrainment in left motor cortex predicts attention-modulated comprehension accuracy.
source: This revealed that entrainment in left motor cortex predicts attention-modulated comprehension accuracy (Figure 4A; Z-difference map at p<0.005).
evidence: This is based on regression analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Individuals with higher levels of comprehension show higher partial coherence in the left motor cortex.
source: This revealed significant positive correlation demonstrating that individuals with higher levels of comprehension show higher partial coherence in the left motor cortex.
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: There is a significant positive correlation between partial coherence in left motor cortex and comprehension accuracy (Pearson's R = 0.38, P = 0.01; Spearman R = 0.32, P = 0.03).
source: Since the accuracy has discrete values such as 70, 80, 90% (correct response rate out of 10 questions at the comprehension testing), we plotted the correlation as a box plot (Figure 4B; Pearson's coefficient of Fisher's Z-transformed data R = 0.38, P = 0.01; Spearman rank correlation R = 0.32, P = 0.03).
evidence: This is based on statistical correlation analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Good performers showed significantly higher partial coherence value in the left motor cortex than poor performers (t42 = 2.2, P = 0.03).
source: Good performers showed significantly higher partial coherence value in the left motor cortex than poor performers (Figure 4C; two-sample t-test on Fisher's Z-transformed data; t42 = 2.2, P = 0.03).
evidence: This is based on group comparison shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Stronger attentional lip entrainment in the left motor cortex supports better speech comprehension.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that stronger attentional lip entrainment in the left motor cortex supports better speech comprehension.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the regression and correlation analyses.

claim: This study provides the first direct evidence that lip movements during continuous speech entrain low-frequency brain oscillations in speech processing brain areas.
source: Here we provide the first direct evidence that lip movements during continuous speech entrain low-frequency brain oscillations in speech processing brain areas, that this entrainment is modulated by attention and congruence, and that entrainment in motor regions correlates with speech comprehension.
evidence: This is stated as the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Detailed information about the identity or specific features of sensory stimuli can be decoded from the low-frequency phase of LFP or MEG/EEG signals.
source: Recent studies provide converging evidence that detailed information about the identity or specific features of sensory stimuli can be decoded from the low-frequency phase of LFP or MEG/EEG signals (Ng et al., 2013; Panzeri et al., 2015; Schyns et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The identity of different audiovisual movie stimuli can be decoded from delta-theta phase in occipital MEG sensors.
source: For example, a recent study has demonstrated that the identity of different audiovisual movie stimuli can be decoded from delta-theta phase in occipital MEG sensors (Luo et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In the auditory domain, stimulus-specificity is at least partly due to a phase synchronization of rhythmic brain activity and the auditory speech envelope.
source: In the auditory domain, this stimulus-specificity is at least partly due to a phase synchronization of rhythmic brain activity and the auditory speech envelope (Gross et al., 2013b; Peelle et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Congruent visual stimulation facilitates auditory speech entrainment.
source: Recent studies have shown that congruent visual stimulation facilitates auditory speech entrainment (Crosse et al., 2015; Zion Golumbic et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Visual entrainment is clearly distinct from auditory entrainment for three reasons: some areas show stronger entrainment to the visual compared than to the auditory stimulus, removing the auditory contribution using partial coherence still results in significant visual entrainment, and there is visual entrainment in the absence of a congruent auditory stimulus.
source: This visual entrainment is clearly distinct from auditory entrainment for three reasons. First, some areas show stronger entrainment to the visual compared than to the auditory stimulus. Second, removing the auditory contribution using partial coherence still results in significant visual entrainment. Third, we report visual entrainment in the absence of a congruent auditory stimulus.
evidence: This is a summary of the evidence supporting the distinctness of visual entrainment.

claim: This study establishes the existence of a visual entrainment mechanism for audiovisual speech in addition to the well-studied auditory entrainment.
source: Together, this establishes the existence of a visual entrainment mechanism for audiovisual speech in addition to the well-studied auditory entrainment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings.

claim: The visual entrainment effect relies on the quasi-rhythmic nature of visual speech that is particularly prominent in the subtle but salient lip movements.
source: In correspondence to the auditory domain, this effect relies on the quasi-rhythmic nature of visual speech that is particularly prominent in the subtle but salient lip movements.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mechanism underlying visual entrainment.

claim: The coherence analysis reveals an extensive network comprising speech processing areas such as bilateral primary sensory areas (V1 and A1), extended sensory visual and auditory areas, posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS), and inferior frontal gyrus (IFG).
source: Our coherence analysis reveals an extensive network comprising speech processing areas such as bilateral primary sensory areas (V1 (Calcarine sulcus; BA 17) and A1 [Heschl's gyrus; BA 41]), extended sensory visual (BA 18/19) and auditory areas (superior/middle temporal gyri; BA 21/22/42), and posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS) as well as inferior frontal gyrus (IFG; BA 44/6).
evidence: This is based on the coherence analysis results.

claim: In occipital areas visual entrainment is significantly stronger compared to auditory entrainment.
source: But as expected, in occipital areas visual entrainment is significantly stronger compared to auditory entrainment.
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of entrainment patterns.

claim: The right superior temporal cortex is significantly stronger coupled to speech envelope than to lip movements while there is no significant difference in left superior temporal cortex.
source: The right superior temporal cortex is significantly stronger coupled to speech envelope than to lip movements while there is no significant difference in left superior temporal cortex.
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of coherence patterns.

claim: Visual speech predominantly entrains left temporal areas (in addition to visual areas).
source: This seems to suggest that visual speech predominantly entrains left temporal areas (in addition to visual areas).
evidence: This is inferred from the asymmetry in auditory areas.

claim: The finding that visual speech predominantly entrains left temporal areas is consistent with a recent fMRI study demonstrating preferential processing of visual speech in left superior temporal areas.
source: This is consistent with a recent fMRI study demonstrating preferential processing of visual speech in left superior temporal areas (Blank and von Kriegstein, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Visual areas are entrained by lip movements and left and right auditory areas by lip movements and speech envelope with only the right auditory cortex showing a stronger coupling to speech envelope compared to lip movements.
source: In summary, we find that visual areas are entrained by lip movements and left and right auditory areas by lip movements and speech envelope with only the right auditory cortex showing a stronger coupling to speech envelope compared to lip movements.
evidence: This is a summary of the entrainment patterns observed.

claim: Attention to visual speech is known to help to disambiguate the competing auditory inputs.
source: Attention to visual speech is known to help to disambiguate the competing auditory inputs (Sumby and Pollack, 1954; Zion Golumbic et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Attention to lip movements leads to significantly increased coupling in left hemispheric visual areas.
source: Interestingly, attention to lip movements leads to significantly increased coupling in left hemispheric visual areas.
evidence: This is based on comparison of attention conditions.

claim: Observers process audiovisual speech preferentially based on information from the left side of a speaker's face (observers' right visual hemifield) as compared to the right side.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that observers process audiovisual speech preferentially based on information from the left side of a speaker's face (observers' right visual hemifield) as compared to the right side (Behne et al., 2008; Campbell et al., 1996; Smeele et al., 1998; Swerts and Krahmer, 2008) (but see Nicholls and Searle, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The preferential processing of the left side of a speaker's face has been related to an attentional bias to the observers' right visual hemifield due to the left hemisphere dominance for speech processing.
source: This has been related to an attentional bias to the observers' right visual hemifield due to the left hemisphere dominance for speech processing (Thompson et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The attentional bias to the right visual hemifield could explain the observed lateralization of entrainment since the right visual hemifield is represented in the left visual cortex.
source: Since the right visual hemifield is represented in the left visual cortex, this attentional bias could explain the observed lateralization of entrainment.
evidence: This is an interpretation linking previous findings to the current results.

claim: The temporal alignment of auditory cortex activity to lip movements is not independent of the congruent acoustic speech stimulus.
source: This seems to suggest that the temporal alignment of auditory cortex activity to lip movements is not independant of the congruent acoustic speech stimulus and therefore speaks against a direct entrainment of auditory cortex activity by lip movements.
evidence: This is inferred from the difference between coherence and partial coherence results.

claim: The informativeness of lip movements significantly modulates the coherence between lip movements and right temporal brain areas.
source: However, the informativeness of lip movements still modulates significantly the coherence between lip movements and right temporal brain areas (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C,D) and indicates an indirect effect of visual attention.
evidence: This is based on coherence analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Left posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS) shows a significant effect of congruence that is only evident in coherence and not in partial coherence map.
source: Similarly, left posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS) shows a significant effect of congruence (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D) that is only evident in coherence and not in partial coherence map.
evidence: This is based on comparison of coherence and partial coherence results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The finding that pSTS shows effects only in coherence is consistent with previous reports of pSTS as a locus of multisensory integration with particular relevance for visual speech recognition.
source: This is consistent with previous reports of pSTS as a locus of multisensory integration (Hocking and Price, 2008; Noesselt et al., 2012) with particular relevance for visual speech recognition (Beauchamp et al., 2004; Blank and von Kriegstein, 2013; Werner and Noppeney, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: There is ample evidence for the activation of left motor cortex during audiovisual speech perception.
source: There is ample evidence for the activation of left motor cortex during audiovisual speech perception (Evans and Davis, 2015; Meister et al., 2007; Mottonen et al., 2013; Watkins et al., 2003; Wilson et al., 2004; Ylinen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Rhythmic audiovisual signals entrain multisensory brain areas and dynamically interact with an internal forward model accessed via the auditory dorsal stream to form dynamically updated predictions that improve further sensory processing.
source: Overall, our findings support an emerging model where rhythmic audiovisual signals entrain multisensory brain areas and dynamically interact with an internal forward model accessed via the auditory dorsal stream to form dynamically updated predictions that improve further sensory processing.
evidence: This is a theoretical model proposed based on the findings.

claim: Brain oscillations might implement inter-subject synchronization and support the surprising efficiency of inter-human communication through entrainment mechanisms.
source: Through these mechanisms brain oscillations might implement inter-subject synchronization and support the surprising efficiency of inter-human communication.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: Data were obtained from 46 healthy subjects (26 females; age range: 18–30 years; mean age: 20.54 ± 2.58 years) and they were all right-handed.
source: Data were obtained from 46 healthy subjects (26 females; age range: 18–30 years; mean age: 20.54 ± 2.58 years) and they were all right-handed confirmed by Edinburgh Handedness Inventory (Oldfield, 1971).
evidence: This is a description of the participant sample.

claim: Two subjects were excluded from the analysis (one subject fell asleep and one had MEG signals with excessive noise), leaving dataset from 44 participants.
source: Two subjects were excluded from the analysis (one subject fell asleep and one had MEG signals with excessive noise). This left dataset from 44 participants (25 females; age range: 18–30 years; mean age: 20.45 ± 2.55 years).
evidence: This describes the final sample after exclusions.

claim: Only native English-speaking volunteers with British nationality were recruited due to the British accent in the stimulus material.
source: Only native English-speaking volunteers with British nationality were recruited due to the British accent in the stimulus material.
evidence: This describes a participant inclusion criterion.

claim: Neuromagnetic signals were obtained with a 248-magnetometers whole-head MEG system using a sampling rate of 1017 Hz.
source: Neuromagnetic signals were obtained with a 248-magnetometers whole-head MEG (Magnetoencephalography) system (MAGNES 3600 WH, 4-D Neuroimaging) in a magnetically shielded room using a sampling rate of 1017 Hz.
evidence: This describes the MEG data acquisition parameters.

claim: The stimuli used in this study were audiovisual video clips of a professional male speaker talking continuously (7–9 min).
source: The stimuli used in this study were audiovisual video clips of a professional male speaker talking continuously (7–9 min).
evidence: This describes the experimental stimuli.

claim: Eleven video clips were filmed by a professional filming company with high-quality audiovisual device and recorded in 1920 x 1080 pixels at 25 fps for video and sampling rate of 48 kHz for audio.
source: Eleven video clips were filmed by a professional filming company with high-quality audiovisual device and recorded in 1920 x 1080 pixels at 25 fps (frame per second) for video and sampling rate of 48 kHz for audio.
evidence: This describes the technical specifications of the stimuli.

claim: In a behavioral study, videos were rated by 33 participants on 9 items using Likert scale 1 to 5, and talks with excessive mean scores were excluded, leaving 8 talks selected for the experiment.
source: In a behavioral study, these videos were rated by 33 participants (19 females; aged 18–31 years; mean age: 22.27 ± 2.64 years) in terms of arousal, familiarity, valence, complexity, significance (informativeness), agreement (persuasiveness), concreteness, self-relatedness, and level of understanding. Participants were instructed to rate each talk on these 9 items using Likert scale (Likert, 1932) 1 to 5 (for an example of concreteness, 1: very abstract, 2: abstract, 3: neither abstract nor concrete, 4: concrete, 5: very concrete). Talks with excessive mean scores (below 1 and over 4) were excluded and 8 talks were selected for the experiment.
evidence: This describes the stimulus validation procedure.

claim: There were no significant differences in the comprehension accuracy between the talks used in the validation study.
source: There were no significant differences in the comprehension accuracy between the talks (mean ± s.e.m. accuracy (%) for talk 1: 84.62 ± 2.91; talk 2: 87.69 ± 2.31; talk 3: 90.77 ± 2.39; talk 4: 85.38 ± 2.43; p>0.05 at all pair-wise t-tests between talks).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the validation data.

claim: There was no significant difference in comprehension accuracy between groups attending to left versus right ear.
source: As expected there was no significant difference in comprehension accuracy between groups (two sample t-test, df: 42, p>0.05) and for the questions addressed here data was pooled across both groups.
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison between groups.

claim: Area and minor axis (representing vertical lip movement) information have almost identical information approaching 1.0 in coherence value.
source: Area and minor axis (representing vertical lip movement) information have almost identical information approaching 1.0 in coherence value (red line; mean ± s.e.m.).
evidence: This is based on coherence analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Major axis information representing horizontal lip movement only does not show similar pattern with either area or minor axis.
source: However, major axis information representing horizontal lip movement only does not show similar pattern with either area or minor axis (purple and blue lines; mean ± s.e.m.).
evidence: This is based on coherence analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Area information was used for further analysis because it represents both horizontal and vertical lip movement.
source: Since area information represents both horizontal and vertical lip movement, we used this information for further analysis.
evidence: This describes the methodological choice for lip signal analysis.
